newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Heavy crudes' bull run ending.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Heavy crudes' bull run ending.

text.p: Asia's heavy-sweet crude prices, which hit 1997 highs last week, were expected to slip this week as cooler Japanese weather prompts buyers to put purchases on hold, traders said on Monday.
"Prices are not crashing, but the bull run seen since July seems to be winding down," said a trader with a Japanese trading company.
In other areas this week, traders said light grades could find some support from a slightly tighter market, while Middle East trading for August was winding down.
Premiums of heavy crudes like Minas and Widuri rose to year high levels of 70 cents per barrel and 50 cents per barrel respectively for August cargoes, while Duri prices reached above ICP +$1.00.
The support for the heavy crudes came mainly from Japanese utility buying. Rapidly rising premiums kept other buyers, such as China and South Korea, out of the market.
But the key Japanese support was now starting to disappear, traders said.
Japanese weather has turned cooler and Japanese utilities have moved to the sidelines, until they get a clearer idea of how hot the summer might be.
Despite the lower Japanese demand, Minas crude may fare slightly better than the other heavy grades, supported by a tighter export market for August, traders said.
Last week, Indonesia said it would allocate for export 38,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) of Minas, compared to 52,000 bpd in July.

Traders said Indonesia was planning to run Minas at its new 65,000-bpd crude distillation unit at the Balikpapan refinery, which is scheduled to come onstream by August, leaving less supplies available for the export market.
But allocations of Duri crude were 31,000 bpd, 55 percent higher than in July.
The volume allocated for Widuri and Cinta crudes, which are interchangeable grades for many refineries, totalled 83,000 bpd, more than double the 34,000 bpd allocated in July.
The ample supplies of Widuri, Cinta and Duri could drag prices down, unless the Japanese weather heats up prompting utilities to resume buying crude for power generation.

In contrast to the heavy crude market, the levels of Asian light sweet grades could stabilise this week, as the movement of cargoes out of the region provides support to an oversupplied market, traders said.
At least two 600,000 barrel cargoes of North West Shelf condensate are headed to the U.S. Gulf Coast, while a total of 850,000 barrels of Cossack and Belida are heading to Hawaii.
Light crudes such as Cossack and Kutubu were traded around Tapis APPI -0.80 cents for August, compared to earlier deals at discounts of more than $1.00.
"I wouldn't say the market is strong, but prices have stopped falling," said a western trader.
